analysis.one_liner: Orders a federal study of hospital contract clauses that block price competition in health care.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would direct a government watchdog to study anti-competitive health insurer contracts, was introduced with no cosponsors and has sat in committee since April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a dominant hospital system negotiates with an insurer, its contract can include clauses that stop the insurer from steering patients to cheaper providers, from tiering doctors by price and quality, or from telling employers and patients what things cost. The bill would not ban anything. It would require the Government Accountability Office, Congress's independent investigative office, to study these four kinds of clauses, list what the Federal Trade Commission and Justice Department have done about them, and assess whether those agencies have the resources to enforce antitrust law against them. The findings and any recommendations would be reported to the House and Senate committees that handle health and competition policy.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary patients would benefit only indirectly, if the study leads to action that lowers prices and improves access. The most immediate beneficiaries are employers and other plan sponsors who pay health bills but often cannot see negotiated rates because of gag clauses, and consumers who could eventually see more price transparency and cheaper in-network options.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying health bills

how_it_helps.text: Requires a study of four contract clauses — anti-steering, anti-tiering, all-or-nothing, and gag clauses — including their effects on industry consolidation, the prices consumers pay for medical services, and consumer access to care.

Requires an inventory of every action the FTC and the Justice Department have taken related to these clauses, plus an assessment of whether those agencies have the resources and capability to enforce antitrust law against them, with recommendations for any needed changes.

The study results must be reported to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Judiciary, and to the Senate Committees on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions and Judiciary, putting the issue formally on those committees' agendas.

By naming and defining each clause type in federal law for the first time, the bill creates a common vocabulary that could anchor future legislation or enforcement against these contracting practices.

analysis.who_pays: If the study eventually leads to restrictions, the cost falls on large hospital systems and consolidated provider networks that rely on these clauses to keep patients inside their networks at negotiated rates. Insurers would give up gag clauses that keep negotiated prices hidden. For now, the only cost is the modest federal cost of the study itself, funded by taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large hospital systems using these clauses

drawbacks.text: The bill only mandates a study; it bans nothing, changes nothing, and directs any actual remedies to a future Congress or to regulators, so patients see no relief even if the practices are as harmful as sponsors contend.
The report is due no later than 18 months after enactment, so even the informational benefit would arrive in late 2026 or later, adding delay on top of the stall in committee.

Hospital systems argue in good faith that some of these clauses serve legitimate purposes: all-or-nothing provisions hold networks together across affiliated facilities, steering restrictions protect care coordination, and tiering rules they contest can reflect genuine quality differences — a study that treats all four as suspect may oversimplify real contract bargaining.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a low-cost, low-impact bill: it spends almost nothing and delivers no direct relief, but it would produce an authoritative factual record on contract practices that raise prices and hide costs from patients and employers. Its real value is as a first step, and its real weakness is that a study alone — especially one with no cosponsors and no committee action — rarely leads anywhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees in April 2025, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill on April 24, 2025.
The same day, the Speaker's referral sent it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, for the relevant provisions, to the Judiciary Committee.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been recorded since the referral, and Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet: hospital systems and insurers keep using these clauses unexamined, and patients and employers get no new information, because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits in committee

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to two House committees for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded opposition or floor vote, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Large hospital systems and consolidated provider networks
industries.note: These systems negotiate anti-steering, anti-tiering, all-or-nothing, and gag clauses that keep patients in their networks and negotiated prices hidden. A study would build the record for restricting them; for now the bill imposes nothing. Sources: S2.

industries.industry: Health insurers and health plan administrators
industries.note: Insurers gain freedom to steer patients to cheaper providers and to tier providers by value if the clauses were restricted, but they have also been parties to gag clauses that hide prices from employers and enrollees. A study alone changes nothing today.

industries.industry: Employers and other plan sponsors of health coverage
industries.note: Gag clauses prevent plan sponsors from learning negotiated rates and allowed amounts, which limits their ability to hold down what they and their workers pay. Disclosure of what the bill studies would work in their favor.

analysis.trajectory: A one-sponsor study bill with no cosponsors and no committee action after referral is very unlikely to move in this Congress unless a committee chair picks it up or it is folded into a larger health package.
